title: Bulb Switcher II
statement:
A row of `n` light bulbs, numbered `1` to `n`, starts with every bulb on. There are four buttons, and each one toggles a fixed group of bulbs (on becomes off, off becomes on):

- Button 1 toggles every bulb.
- Button 2 toggles the bulbs with an even number (2, 4, 6, ...).
- Button 3 toggles the bulbs with an odd number (1, 3, 5, ...).
- Button 4 toggles the bulbs whose number is one more than a multiple of 3 (1, 4, 7, 10, ...).

You press buttons exactly `presses` times in total, choosing any of the four buttons each time (the same button may be chosen again). Return how many different on/off patterns of the whole row can be left after all `presses` presses.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating every sequence of presses explodes, but two facts shrink the problem to a handful of cases.

- **Only parity matters.** Toggles commute and pressing a button twice undoes it, so a sequence is described by which buttons were pressed an odd number of times: at most 16 combinations.
- **Only the first three bulbs matter.** Bulb 5 always matches bulb 3, bulb 6 matches bulb 2, the row repeats every 6 bulbs, and bulb 4 equals bulb 1 XOR bulb 2 XOR bulb 3. So a pattern is fixed by bulbs 1–3, and there are at most 8 patterns.

With `presses` presses, a set of odd-pressed buttons is reachable when its size is at most `presses` and has the same parity. Counting the distinct patterns those sets produce on `min(n, 3)` bulbs gives a small table.

## Approach

1. With no presses only the all-on row exists: return 1.
2. Set `bulbs = min(n, 3)`.
3. One bulb: it can be on or off, so 2.
4. Two bulbs: one press gives 3 rows (all four buttons cannot make "on, on"); two or more give all 4.
5. Three or more bulbs: one press gives 4 rows, two presses give 7 (every row except the one button 4 alone makes), three or more give all 8.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 1`, `presses = 1`. `presses` is not 0, `bulbs = min(1, 3) = 1`, so the answer is `2`: button 1 turns the bulb off, button 2 leaves it on.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1): a few comparisons.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- `presses = 0` returns 1 for every `n`; check it before anything else.
- Two presses on three bulbs give 7, not 8: the row button 4 alone makes can otherwise only come from pressing all four buttons once, which takes four presses.
- Presses are exactly `presses`, not "at most", which is why the parity of the count matters.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of bulbs |
| `presses` | exact number of button presses |
| `bulbs` | `min(n, 3)`, the bulbs that decide the whole pattern |

narration.2: With no presses at all, nothing changes.
narration.5: Bulbs 4 onward are determined by bulbs 1 to 3, so at most three bulbs matter.
narration.6: A single bulb can only be on or off.
narration.7: Both states are reachable with any positive number of presses.
narration.9: Two bulbs give at most four rows.
narration.10: One press cannot keep both bulbs on; two or more presses reach all four rows.
narration.12: Three or more bulbs with one press: each button gives its own row.
narration.13: The four buttons give four different rows.
narration.15: Two presses miss the row of button 4 alone; three or more reach all eight rows.
